venues.name: Four Seasons Hotel Firenze
venues.note: A restored 15th-century Medici palace wrapped around the city's largest private garden, the finest address in Florence, without argument.
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 9, highest in Florence)

venues.name: Hotel Savoy, a Rocco Forte Hotel
venues.note: The grande dame of the city centre, on Florence's grandest square, pure Rocco Forte polish, steps from the Duomo.

venues.name: The St. Regis Florence
venues.note: A Brunelleschi-designed Renaissance palace on the Arno, St. Regis butler service inside a piece of the city's history.

venues.name: Villa San Michele, A Belmond Hotel, Florence
venues.note: A former monastery with a façade attributed to Michelangelo's school, looking down on the whole of Florence from Fiesole.

venues.name: Portrait Firenze, Lungarno Collection
venues.note: The Ferragamo family's jewel steps from the Ponte Vecchio, a small, exacting house with the best river address in the city.
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World

venues.name: Helvetia & Bristol Firenze, Starhotels Collezione
venues.note: The first grand hotel in the historic centre, a 19th-century townhouse on the fashion street, run with quiet Florentine grace.
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World

venues.name: Collegio alla Querce, Auberge Resorts Collection
venues.note: A 16th-century former boarding school on the hillside, reborn as Auberge's first Italian house, the city's newest icon.
credentials: Architectural Digest, Great Design Hotel Award (2025)
MICHELIN Guide, Best New Hotels in the World

venues.name: Palazzo Portinari Salviati, Residenza d'Epoca
venues.note: Frescoed rooms in the 15th-century home of Dante's Beatrice, later Cosimo I de' Medici's own residence.

venues.name: Villa Cora
venues.note: A 19th-century aristocratic villa above the Boboli Gardens, belle-époque grandeur with a pool and its own park.

venues.name: Villa La Massa
venues.note: A 16th-century Medici villa on the Arno just beyond the city, Villa d'Este's Tuscan sister, riverside and serene.
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World

venues.name: Il Salviatino Firenze
venues.note: A converted 15th-century villa high in the Fiesole hills, with frescoes, terraced gardens and the city laid out below.

venues.name: Hotel Lungarno, Lungarno Collection
venues.note: The Ferragamos' riverside house on the Oltrarno bank, hung with a private art collection and looking to the Ponte Vecchio.

venues.name: Brunelleschi Hotel
venues.note: Built into a 6th-century Byzantine tower and medieval church, in a hidden square a lane from the Duomo.

venues.name: The Place Firenze
venues.note: A discreet, residence-like boutique by Santa Maria Novella, more private home than hotel, and all the better for it.

venues.name: Palazzo Vecchietti
venues.note: A 16th-century palace turned all-suite house, Michele Bonan interiors, each room named for a Florentine artist.
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World

venues.name: Grand Hotel Minerva
venues.note: The only rooftop pool with a Duomo view in the centre, above a 13th-century palazzo on Santa Maria Novella square.

venues.name: COMO Castello del Nero
venues.note: A restored Renaissance castle in the Chianti hills, the COMO group's Tuscan estate, a short drive from the city.

venues.name: Riva Lofts Florence
venues.note: A 19th-century factory turned green, sleepy retreat on the quiet bank of the Arno, gently removed from the crowds.

venues.name: Velona's Jungle Luxury Suites
venues.note: A jewel-box of maximalist design in the historic centre, small, bold and full of personality.

venues.name: Torre di Bellosguardo
venues.note: A medieval tower and Renaissance villa on the Bellosguardo hill, with the most storied private view of Florence.

venues.name: Hotel Calimala
venues.note: A polished contemporary boutique metres from the Duomo, with a rooftop terrace over the rooftops.

venues.name: Ad Astra
venues.note: A quiet villa-hotel set in Europe's largest privately owned walled garden, on the Oltrarno bank.

venues.name: NH Collection Firenze Porta Rossa
venues.note: One of Italy's oldest hotels, in a medieval tower a lane from the Ponte Vecchio, history at a sensible price.

venues.name: Enoteca Pinchiorri
venues.note: Florence's only three-star, in a 17th-century palazzo, three stars held since 2004, and one of Europe's great wine cellars.

venues.name: Santa Elisabetta
venues.note: A jewel-box two-star inside a Byzantine tower at the Brunelleschi Hotel, Tuscan produce, exactingly rendered.

venues.name: Gucci Osteria da Massimo Bottura
venues.note: Bottura's playful, worldly kitchen on the city's grandest square, Karime Lopez and Takahiko Kondo cooking with real wit.

venues.name: Il Palagio
venues.note: Refined, produce-led cooking in the Four Seasons' neoclassical rooms, opening onto the great garden.

venues.name: Borgo San Jacopo
venues.note: A star with two balcony tables over the Arno, looking straight at the Ponte Vecchio, the finest river view in the city.

venues.name: Atto di Vito Mollica
venues.note: Vito Mollica's frescoed room behind the cathedral, sea-led, considered cooking in a Medici palace.

venues.name: Saporium Firenze
venues.note: Ariel Hagen's sustainable, garden-to-plate cooking on the Arno's quieter bank, Tuscany at its most seasonal.

venues.name: Serrae Villa Fiesole
venues.note: Vito Mollica's second star in the Fiesole hills, modern, refined cooking with the whole valley below.

venues.name: Luca's by Paulo Airaudo
venues.note: Airaudo's newly-starred kitchen at Hotel La Gemma, inventive, precise cooking in the heart of the city.

venues.name: Ora d'Aria
venues.note: Marco Stabile's long-standing modern-Tuscan room near the Ponte Vecchio, a Florence fixture of real craft.

venues.name: Cibrèo Ristorante
venues.note: The elegant flagship of the Cibrèo family, Florence's iconic dishes, cooked with warmth and no pretence.

venues.name: Trattoria Cibrèo, Il Cibrèino
venues.note: The trattoria sibling of Cibrèo, the same iconic cooking, a fraction of the ceremony, and no reservations.

venues.name: Il Santo Bevitore
venues.note: A convivial Oltrarno room of cured meats, ribollita and roast pigeon, Tuscan classics done exactly right.

venues.name: Il Latini
venues.note: A fourth-generation fiaschetteria from 1911, hams from the ceiling, communal tables, and Tuscany on every plate.

venues.name: Zeb
venues.note: A tiny mother-and-son counter in San Niccolò serving creative Tuscan cooking to a handful of stools.

venues.name: Trattoria Cammillo
venues.note: A beloved 1945 trattoria near the Ponte Vecchio, Tuscan classics with a worldly twist, run by the same family for decades.

venues.name: Buca Lapi
venues.note: The oldest cellar restaurant in Florence, since 1880, the home of a proper bistecca alla fiorentina.

venues.name: La Giostra
venues.note: A theatrical, candlelit Santa Croce trattoria of great generosity, pasta, pici and a famous warmth of welcome.

venues.name: Trattoria Sostanza
venues.note: A working trattoria since 1869, no reservations, shared tables, and the butter chicken Florence queues for.

venues.name: Cibrèo Caffè
venues.note: The Cibrèo family's café, modern, reimagined local cooking in a relaxed, all-day setting.

venues.name: L'Ortone
venues.note: Contemporary cooking on traditional Tuscan foundations, beside the city's oldest food market.

venues.name: Podere 39
venues.note: A secret-garden trattoria on the city's southern edge, meat, fish and vegetables cooked with real care.

venues.name: Trattoria da Burde
venues.note: A love-letter-to-Tuscany trattoria on the outskirts, old-fashioned, generous, and worth the short trip.

venues.name: Trattoria da Bibe
venues.note: A countryside family trattoria south of the city, Tuscan home cooking exactly as it should be.

venues.name: La Torre, COMO Castello del Nero
venues.note: Refined Tuscan cooking inside a Renaissance castle in the Chianti hills, a destination in its own right.

venues.name: Florence Cathedral (Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore)
venues.note: The green, pink and white marble bulk of Florence's cathedral is the city's beating heart, its nave vast enough to swallow a crowd yet hushed under Brunelleschi's dome. Entry to the cathedral floor is free, so a multi-generational group can step inside together at their own pace, and a private early guide sidesteps the queues that ring the piazza by mid-morning.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Brunelleschi's Dome (Cupola del Duomo)
venues.note: Still the largest masonry dome ever raised, built between 1420 and 1436 without scaffolding by a technique Brunelleschi kept secret. The 463-step climb between its double shells rewards you with the Vasari-Zuccari Last Judgement frescoes at eye level and all of Florence at your feet, timed-entry only, best booked well ahead through your advisor for a first slot.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Florence Baptistery (Battistero di San Giovanni)
venues.note: The octagonal Romanesque baptistery is among the oldest buildings in the city, its ceiling a shimmering gold-ground mosaic of the Last Judgement that reduces most visitors to silence. Ghiberti's bronze 'Gates of Paradise' face the cathedral, the originals now protected in the Opera del Duomo museum, with faithful casts in place here.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Giotto's Campanile (Campanile di Giotto)
venues.note: Giotto's slender bell tower, sheathed in the same white, green and red marble as the cathedral, is widely held to be the most beautiful in Italy. Its 414 steps open onto terraces that frame the dome itself, the one climb in Florence that puts Brunelleschi's cupola in your photograph rather than under your feet.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Museo dell'Opera del Duomo
venues.note: The quietest and most rewarding stop of the whole cathedral complex, holding the original sculptures moved indoors for safekeeping, Ghiberti's real Gates of Paradise, Donatello's gaunt Magdalene, and Michelangelo's unfinished Bandini Pietà. A full-scale reconstruction of the cathedral's medieval facade fills a light-filled hall, making this an air-conditioned, unhurried refuge for older travellers.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Uffizi Gallery (Le Gallerie degli Uffizi)
venues.note: The single greatest concentration of Renaissance painting on earth, from Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera to Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael and Caravaggio, hung in Vasari's Medici office block above the Arno. It rewards a private early-access or after-hours guide who can walk you to the essentials in two focused hours rather than three exhausting ones.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Galleria dell'Accademia (Michelangelo's David)
venues.note: You come for one thing, Michelangelo's David, luminous under his purpose-built skylight, and stay for the unfinished 'Prisoners' straining out of their marble blocks nearby, a lesson in genius no photograph conveys. Small enough for a short, comfortable visit with children or grandparents; reserved timed entry is essential year-round.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Bargello National Museum (Museo Nazionale del Bargello)
venues.note: Florence's finest sculpture collection sits in a 13th-century fortress-palace and is almost always calm, Donatello's bronze David, his St. George, works by Michelangelo, Verrocchio and Cellini, and the two competing baptistery-door panels that launched the Renaissance. The connoisseur's alternative to the crowds, and blessedly cool in summer.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Palazzo Vecchio
venues.note: Florence's fortress town hall still governs the city, its Salone dei Cinquecento a golden hall of Vasari battle frescoes and a Michelangelo 'Genius of Victory'. Family-friendly 'secret passages' tours climb into hidden staircases and the roof timbers, and the tower gives a view that is pure medieval Florence, a rare place where children and adults are equally gripped.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Piazza della Signoria & Loggia dei Lanzi
venues.note: Florence's open-air sculpture court and its living room for seven centuries, ringed by Cellini's bronze Perseus, Giambologna's Rape of the Sabine Women and a copy of David on the spot the original once stood. Ideal for an unhurried evening passeggiata, with Rivoire's historic cafe on the square for hot chocolate after dark.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Ponte Vecchio
venues.note: The last of Florence's bridges to survive the war, lined since the 1590s with goldsmiths and jewellers whose little shuttered shops overhang the Arno. Cross it at dawn or after the day-trippers leave for the honeyed light the painters loved; the goldsmiths remain a discreet place to commission a bespoke piece.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Vasari Corridor (Corridoio Vasariano)
venues.note: The Medici's private elevated passage, built by Vasari in 1565 so the family could walk from the Uffizi to the Pitti Palace above the crowds and over the Ponte Vecchio. Reopened to the public in December 2024 after long restoration, it is one of the most exclusive walks in Italy, best arranged as a small-group or private slot through your advisor.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Pitti Palace (Palazzo Pitti)
venues.note: The Medici and later Savoy grand-ducal residence across the river, now a cluster of museums, the Palatine Gallery hangs Raphaels and Titians three-deep in gilded state rooms, alongside the Treasury, costume and modern-art collections. A single palace that can absorb a whole leisurely day, with plenty of seating for those who tire of walking.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Boboli Gardens (Giardino di Boboli)
venues.note: The Medici's monumental hillside garden behind the Pitti, a 16th-century blueprint for the formal gardens of Europe, terraced with fountains, statue-lined avenues and the grotto of Buontalenti. Green, shaded and expansive, the natural place to rest a multi-generational group between museums, with panoramas back over the city.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Bardini Garden (Giardino Bardini)
venues.note: A steep, little-known garden whose Baroque staircase and springtime wisteria tunnel frame one of the most beautiful and least crowded views of the Florence skyline. The villa's terrace cafe is a serene, discreet spot for lunch or an aperitivo away from the centre's bustle.

venues.name: Piazzale Michelangelo
venues.note: The classic panorama of Florence, the whole terracotta city and its dome laid out across the Arno, from a 19th-century terrace by Giuseppe Poggi. Best at sunset or, for a group who prefers calm, at first light; a private car up the hill spares elderly travellers the climb.

venues.name: Basilica of San Miniato al Monte
venues.note: One of the oldest and most atmospheric churches in Tuscany, its green-and-white Romanesque facade crowning the hill just above Piazzale Michelangelo. The Benedictine monks still sing Gregorian chant at vespers, a quietly moving experience, and the terrace view rivals the piazzale below with a fraction of the crowd.

venues.name: Basilica of Santa Croce
venues.note: The great Franciscan church and the pantheon of Italian genius, holding the tombs of Michelangelo, Galileo, Machiavelli and Rossini, with Giotto frescoes in the chapels and Brunelleschi's serene Pazzi Chapel in the cloister. The leather school behind the apse (below) makes this a natural pairing of art and craft.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Basilica of San Lorenzo & Medici Chapels
venues.note: The Medici's parish church, its facade left raw but its interior a Brunelleschi masterpiece, with Michelangelo's Laurentian Library staircase alongside. The attached Medici Chapels hold the dynasty's marble tombs carved by Michelangelo himself, Dawn, Dusk, Night and Day, beneath a chapel of inlaid semiprecious stone.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Basilica of Santa Maria Novella
venues.note: The Dominicans' church, with Alberti's mathematically perfect marble facade and Masaccio's revolutionary 'Trinity', the first true painting in Renaissance perspective. Steps away sits its ancient pharmacy (below), making the quarter around the station a surprisingly rich pocket of the city.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella
venues.note: The world's oldest pharmacy, founded by Dominican friars in 1221 and still compounding fragrances, tonics and rosewater in frescoed, chandeliered salons off Via della Scala. Part museum, part boutique, a discreet, unhurried place to choose gifts, with private appointments and shipping easily arranged.

venues.name: Brancacci Chapel (Cappella Brancacci)
venues.note: A small chapel inside Santa Maria del Carmine holding Masaccio's frescoes of St Peter, the cycle that taught the entire Renaissance how to paint volume and emotion, studied by Michelangelo as a young man. Timed, small-group entry keeps it intimate; an art-historian guide turns a ten-minute stop into the highlight of a trip.

venues.name: Basilica of Santo Spirito
venues.note: Brunelleschi's last and purest church, its plain 18th-century facade hiding a sublime, perfectly proportioned interior, and a small wooden crucifix carved by a teenage Michelangelo. The tree-lined piazza outside is the social heart of the Oltrarno, ringed with wine bars and trattorie that fill at aperitivo hour.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Palazzo Davanzati (Museum of the Old Florentine House)
venues.note: A rare intact 14th-century merchant's palace, its frescoed 'Hall of Parrots' and 'Peacock Room' showing exactly how a wealthy Florentine family lived between the medieval tower and the Renaissance palazzo. Small, calm and endlessly atmospheric, a hidden gem that lets a family picture daily life behind all the marble grandeur.

venues.name: Medici Riccardi Palace & Gozzoli Chapel
venues.note: The Medici's first family palace, its tiny private chapel entirely wrapped in Benozzo Gozzoli's jewel-like 'Procession of the Magi', a fresco parade of the family themselves in Renaissance finery. Timed entry keeps the chapel serene, one of the most dazzling small rooms in all of Florence.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: San Marco Museum (Museo di San Marco)
venues.note: A Dominican convent where Fra Angelico painted a devotional fresco in every monk's cell, including the ethereal 'Annunciation' at the top of the stairs. Quiet, contemplative and rarely crowded, many consider it the most spiritually affecting museum in the city, and Savonarola's own cell survives here.

venues.name: Mercato Centrale & San Lorenzo Market
venues.note: A soaring 19th-century iron market hall whose ground floor is Florence's larder and whose upper floor is a bustling gourmet food court open late, pasta, gelato, wine and, importantly, several genuinely good vegetarian and produce-forward stalls for veg-aware travellers. The leather stalls of the surrounding streets are the city's classic shopping scrum.

venues.name: Sant'Ambrogio Market
venues.note: The neighbourhood market where Florentines actually shop, far calmer than San Lorenzo, with a covered hall of cheese, produce and flowers and a beloved cluster of no-frills lunch spots outside. The authentic, unstaged side of the city for anyone who has already seen the sights and wants to feel the daily rhythm.

venues.name: Scuola del Cuoio (Leather School of Santa Croce)
venues.note: Founded after the war by Franciscan friars and Florentine leather families inside the monastery behind Santa Croce, still the city's largest working leather workshop where you watch artisans cut, tool and gild by hand. Bespoke bags and small goods can be commissioned and monogrammed on the spot, a memorable, hands-on stop that engages every generation.

venues.name: Oltrarno Artisan Quarter (San Frediano & Santo Spirito)
venues.note: The 'other side of the Arno' where Florence's craft still lives, book-binders, gilders, silversmiths, frame-makers and cobblers in tiny street-level botteghe along Via Maggio, Via dei Serragli and Borgo San Frediano. A private artisan walk arranges introductions inside the workshops that don't advertise, the quiet luxury of being let behind the door.

venues.name: Gucci Garden (Gucci Museum) & Piazza della Signoria fashion houses
venues.note: Florence is the birthplace of Italian fashion, and the Gucci Garden on the Piazza della Signoria pairs an archive-museum of the house's Florentine roots with a Massimo Bottura restaurant. A civilised pause for design-minded travellers between the Uffizi and Palazzo Vecchio, moments from the Ferragamo museum across the river.

venues.name: Museo Ferragamo (Palazzo Spini Feroni)
venues.note: Inside Salvatore Ferragamo's medieval-palace flagship on Via de' Tornabuoni, a museum of the shoemaker-to-the-stars' inventions and Hollywood commissions. Set on Florence's most elegant shopping street, the natural base for a discreet afternoon among the maisons of Via de' Tornabuoni.

venues.name: Rose Garden & Iris Garden (Giardino delle Rose)
venues.note: A free, gently terraced garden just below Piazzale Michelangelo with a thousand rose varieties, Folon bronze sculptures and the same city view without the tour-bus crowd. The adjacent Iris Garden blooms only in May, when Florence's emblem flower fills the hillside, a serene, romantic spot to catch your breath.

venues.name: Basilica of Santissima Annunziata & Piazza SS. Annunziata
venues.note: Florence's most harmonious Renaissance square, framed by Brunelleschi's Ospedale degli Innocenti, Europe's first orphanage and the first truly Renaissance building, with its Della Robbia roundels of swaddled infants. A moving, under-visited corner with a small museum, and the square's arcades give welcome shade.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Santa Trinita & the Sassetti Chapel
venues.note: An easily missed church at the foot of Via de' Tornabuoni holding Ghirlandaio's fresco cycle of St Francis, painted against a recognisable 15th-century Florentine skyline peopled with real Medici-era faces. A quick, rich stop that rewards the shopper detouring off Tornabuoni.

venues.name: Galileo Museum (Museo Galileo)
venues.note: A dazzling collection of Renaissance and Medici scientific instruments, antique globes, astrolabes, telescopes and, disarmingly, Galileo's own preserved finger. A refreshing change of register from the paintings, and a genuine hit with curious children and grandchildren, right by the Uffizi on the river.

venues.name: Stibbert Museum (Museo Stibbert)
venues.note: The eccentric hilltop villa of a Victorian collector, its halls filled with a life-size cavalcade of European and Japanese armour and a romantic English garden. Well off the tourist track and reachable by a short private drive, an unexpected, atmospheric outing for a group that has done the Renaissance headliners.

venues.name: Chianti Classico wine estates (Greve, Radda, Castellina)
venues.note: The rolling cypress-and-vine country between Florence and Siena, where historic family estates and Antinori's cathedral-like modern winery pour Chianti Classico and Super Tuscans over long lunches. A private-driver day with a pre-arranged cellar visit and estate meal is the discreet way to do it, the kitchens will happily cook Tuscan vegetarian on notice.

venues.name: Antinori nel Chianti Classico (winery & estate)
venues.note: The Antinori family's architecturally striking headquarters, a spiralling glass-and-terracotta winery buried in the hillside with a rooftop of vines, a museum and a restaurant over the barrel halls. Just 30 minutes from the city, the most polished single wine visit near Florence, and easily booked as a private experience.

venues.name: Siena (Piazza del Campo & Duomo)
venues.note: The great medieval rival to Florence, built in warm brick around the shell-shaped Piazza del Campo and crowned by a zebra-striped cathedral of astonishing marble floors. A private day-trip lets an older group tour the Campo and Duomo unhurried and lunch well before the return, Tuscan cuisine here is generous to vegetarians.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Siena

venues.name: Chianti hot-air balloon & vineyard sunrise
venues.note: A dawn balloon flight over the vine-striped Chianti hills, drifting silently above castles and cypress avenues before a Champagne-and-Tuscan breakfast on landing. A rare, once-in-a-trip experience arranged privately for a family or couple, weather-dependent, so build flexibility into the itinerary.

venues.name: Cooking class & market experience in a Tuscan villa
venues.note: A private chef-led class, often paired with a morning at Sant'Ambrogio market, turning fresh Tuscan produce into handmade pasta, ribollita and dolci in a countryside kitchen. Fully adaptable to vegetarian and Jain-friendly requests with advance notice, and a warm, hands-on afternoon that brings multiple generations together around one table.

venues.name: Cathedral rooftop & 'Terraces' guided walk
venues.note: A small-group guided route across the cathedral's usually-closed exterior terraces and galleries, walking around the base of the dome at rooftop height among the marble sculpture up close. An exclusive, vertigo-light alternative for those who'd rather not climb 463 steps but still want the intimacy of Brunelleschi's masterpiece.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Florence

venues.name: Locale Firenze
venues.note: A 16th-century palace turned world-class cocktail bar, Renaissance rooms, cutting-edge mixology, and Italy's highest-ranked bar.
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 22, highest in Italy)

venues.name: Gucci Giardino 25
venues.note: A stylish Gucci-designed bar on the city's grandest square, aperitivo and classics with real polish.

venues.name: Empireo, Plaza Hotel Lucchesi
venues.note: A rooftop with a near-360° sweep of the city, the Duomo, the Arno and the domes, cocktail in hand.
credentials: A landmark rooftop bar, atop the Plaza Hotel Lucchesi

venues.name: La Terrazza, Hotel Continentale (Lungarno Collection)
venues.note: The Ferragamos' rooftop over the Ponte Vecchio, the most romantic aperitivo terrace in the city.
credentials: A landmark rooftop bar, Lungarno Collection

venues.name: Caffè Rivoire
venues.note: An 1872 institution on Piazza della Signoria, the grand aperitivo, and the city's most famous hot chocolate.

venues.name: Manifattura
venues.area: Centro Storico / near Piazza della Repubblica
venues.note: A retro bar serving only Italian spirits, vermouth, amari and gin, in a proper mid-century Florentine mood.
credentials: A noted Florence cocktail bar, all-Italian spirits

venues.name: Rasputin
venues.note: A hidden 1920s-style speakeasy behind an unmarked door, Florence's cult after-dark cocktail den.
credentials: A noted Florence speakeasy cocktail bar
